Guided trip

The constellations

Twelve figures of the night sky, drawn star by star. Leaving goes back to Earth.

Open the trip: The constellations

Orion, the hunter

Three stars in a row and four more around them: the easiest figure in the sky to find, and one that both halves of the world can see. The Greeks drew a hunter here. In Egypt it was the god Osiris, and across Latin America the three belt stars are the Three Marys.

Orion, seen from the side

Now leave home. Bellatrix, the hunter's shoulder, is two hundred and fifty light-years from us. Betelgeuse is five hundred, and the middle star of the belt nearly two thousand. The hunter is a line of sight, not a place: from here, hundreds of light-years to one side, nobody would draw him.

The bull and the Seven Sisters

Follow Orion's belt up and to the right and you reach the orange eye of the bull, Aldebaran, and past it a small knot of blue stars. They are the Pleiades, a real family of stars that were born together. Japan calls them Subaru, and for Māori their return before dawn, as Matariki, begins the new year.

The twins

Two bright stars side by side, Castor and Pollux, are the heads of twin brothers standing in the Milky Way. They only look like twins. Pollux is an orange giant thirty-four light-years away. Castor is fifty-one, and is really six stars circling one another.

The lion

A backwards question mark for the mane and a triangle for the hindquarters: the lion is one of the few figures that looks like its name. The bright star at its chest is Regulus, the little king. The Sun passes right beside it every August.

The Plough, and the way north

Seven stars that Britain calls the Plough, America the Big Dipper and much of Europe a wagon: they are the back and tail of the Great Bear. Take the two stars at the end of the bowl and follow them up, five times their own gap. That lone star is Polaris, and it sits almost exactly over the Earth's north pole.

Cassiopeia, across the pole

Go straight on past Polaris, as far again, and you meet a letter W of five stars: Cassiopeia, a queen in the Greek story. She and the Plough sit on opposite sides of the pole and swing round it like the two ends of a seesaw, so when one is low the other is high.

The Summer Triangle

Three bright stars from three different figures: Vega in the Lyre, Deneb in the Swan, Altair in the Eagle. The pale band running between them is the Milky Way, shown as a long exposure would catch it. In China it is the Silver River, which parts the Weaver Girl, Vega, from the Cowherd, Altair.

The scorpion

A red heart, and a long curved tail with a sting at the end. The heart is Antares, a star so large that it would swallow the orbit of Mars. In the Greek story this is the scorpion that killed Orion, which is why the two are never in the sky together. In Hawaii the same stars are the fish hook of Maui.

The teapot, and the centre of the galaxy

The archer's brightest stars make a teapot, and the Milky Way rises from its spout like steam. Look just past the spout and you are looking at the centre of our galaxy, about twenty-seven thousand light-years away, hidden behind dust. Every star named on this trip is in our own small corner of it.

The Southern Cross

The smallest of the eighty-eight constellations, and the best known south of the equator. Australia, New Zealand, Brazil, Papua New Guinea and Samoa all fly it on their flags. The two bright stars beside it are the Pointers, and the nearer is Alpha Centauri, the closest star system to the Sun. The dark patch at the foot of the Cross is the head of the Emu that Aboriginal Australians see in the Milky Way.

The zodiac

The dashed line is the path the Sun takes across the stars in a year. The Moon and the planets never stray far from it, because the Solar System is nearly flat. The figures along it are the zodiac. Babylonian sky watchers counted twelve; the line really crosses thirteen, and the one left out is here: Ophiuchus, the serpent bearer.

Everything is drawn where it really is, from the HYG star database and the planets’ own orbits (astronomy-engine).
